concepts.title: A backup and the working folder are separate
concepts.text: An archive holds saved file contents and permissions. Restoring the whole archive can overwrite newer work, so first decide which file actually needs recovery.

concepts.title: Name the member and its destination
concepts.text: tar -t lists stored names. In tar -x -f ARCHIVE -C PARENT MEMBER, -x restores, -f names the archive, -C chooses a destination parent, and MEMBER is the exact stored name, including its top folder.

concepts.title: Inspect the result
concepts.text: cat reads the restored text. stat -c '%a %U %G' PATH shows its simulated permissions, owner and group: %a chooses the octal permission number, %U the owner name and %G the group name. Quotes keep this format together as one argument. Check compares actual contents and metadata and also looks for unrelated changes.

concepts.title: An increment is not a complete copy
concepts.text: After the base, an incremental archive stores changed or new files and information about directory membership. It can omit unchanged files; the newest archive is not necessarily enough. These are GNU tar-style incremental backups: -g and -G are GNU extensions, not portable options for every tar implementation.

concepts.title: Restore from oldest to newest
concepts.text: Start with the full base, then apply each needed increment in order. Reversing levels can put old text back. Skipping a middle level can lose a change that never appeared in a later archive.

concepts.title: Deletion needs directory information
concepts.text: In this subset tar -xGf restores incremental directory inventories as well as file data. Without -G or -g /dev/null, extraction is an ordinary overlay and may retain names that were deleted at backup time.

concepts.title: A snapshot remembers what was saved
concepts.text: In tar -c -f ARCHIVE -g SNAPSHOT, -c creates an archive, -f names the output archive and -g names the tracking snapshot. That snapshot records which names and changes were seen; creating a backup updates it. It is tracking data, not the backup payload itself.

concepts.title: A branch needs a copy of the intended base
concepts.text: Copy the older snapshot to a new name before making a branch. Starting from a later snapshot can omit earlier changes that a base-plus-branch recovery still needs.

concepts.title: Verify from the declared starting point
concepts.text: A current working folder can hide missing payloads. The checks rebuild base plus branch on separate sample inputs as well as inspecting the verification folder.

An earlier good-looking restore does not prove the delivered archive works.
